titleStmt.title: Response-Time Analysis for Limited-Preemptive Self-Suspending and Event-Driven Delay-Induced Tasks

analytic.title: Response-Time Analysis for Limited-Preemptive Self-Suspending and Event-Driven Delay-Induced Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Heterogeneous computing platforms running highly parallelized applications are becoming increasingly common in real-time embedded systems. This demands for expressive task models that can capture parallelism, precedence constraints and self-suspending behavior caused by work-offloading on coprocessors, access to shared resources or synchronization between tasks running on different (heterogeneous) cores. The Event-Driven Delay-induced (EDD) task model was specifically designed to address these needs. Yet, to date, a single schedulability test for the EDD task model exists, and that test is limited to the analysis of fully-preemptive partitioned scheduling.

In this work, we provide the first worst-case response time analysis for limited-preemptive EDD tasks that are globally scheduled on a multicore platform. Moreover, our evaluation results show that our analysis also outperforms the state-of-theart response time analyses for both limited-preemptive DAG tasks and self-suspending tasks.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Heterogeneous platforms integrating multicore processors together with hardware accelerators are increasingly common in embedded real-time systems. Those platforms allow running complex and data-intensive applications under high-performance and energy efficiency requirements. Assisted driving, smart manufacturing, robotics, and autonomous drones are just a few examples of applications that make use of such platforms nowadays. Those applications are required to perform data-intensive processing and execute multiple tasks (e.g., sensor fusion, planning, control) parallelized across different computing resources (e.g., multiple cores, GPU, TPU, FPGA). This results in complex timing dependencies between tasks running on different computing resources.

Two models have been typically used in the real-time systems literature to analyze such complex applications: selfsuspending tasks and DAG tasks. On the one hand, selfsuspending tasks allow to model tasks that offload workload to other computing resources and suspend their execution while waiting for the results of the offloaded computation. On the other hand, DAG tasks allow to model the dependencies between the execution of parallel segments of an application by explicitly specifying which segments can run in parallel, and which segments must respect precedence constraints due to data or control flow dependencies. Recently, [1] introduced a new model integrating the self-suspending and DAG task models. This new model is called the Event-Driven Delayinduced (EDD) task model. Like DAG tasks, EDD tasks are modeled as a directed-acyclic graph (DAG) where edges between nodes in the graph represent precedence constraints between different execution segments of the task. However, different from DAG tasks, the edges of an EDD task also represent delays between the end of the execution of one segment and the earliest time at which the next segment may start executing (like in the segmented self-suspending task model). An EDD task can thus model precedence constraints, parallelism, and delays caused by waiting for data from an I/O, a sensor, or a GPU, or waiting for the completion of or acknowledgment by a job executing on another processor. The EDD task model is therefore ideal to model the asynchronous execution of parallel jobs on heterogeneous platforms.

State-of-the-art schedulability analyses for DAG, selfsuspended, and EDD tasks are mostly focused on fully preemptive scheduling. However, the execution time of dataintensive applications is often susceptible to the availability of their data in cache and main memory. Their performance may thus be very negatively impacted by data evictions caused by preemptions by other tasks. Therefore, it was argued [2] that limited-preemptive scheduling is a more suitable solution to meet the timing and performance requirements of such applications since it allows executing critical execution segments non-preemptively and restricts preemptions to occur only between segments with limited data dependency.

There exist only two schedulability analyses for nonpreemptive self-suspending tasks [3], [4]. The analysis by Casini et al. [4] is limited to single core scheduling, or partitioned scheduling on multicore platforms. The analysis by Yalcinkaya et al. [3] uses UPPAAL to analyze segmented selfsuspending tasks executed with global fixed-priority scheduling on a multicore platform. The test in [3] is an exact schedulability analysis but it does not return bounds on the worst-case response time (WCRT) of the tasks. Foughali et al. [5] propose another UPPAAL-based test for limited-Criterion Casini [4] Yalcinkaya [3] SAG [7] Foughali [5] This paper WCRT

The only existing analysis for the generalized EDD task model was proposed by Aromolo et al. [1]. It proposes a response time analysis for preemptive fixed-priority partitioned scheduling on multicore platforms. To date, there is no analysis for non-preemptive or limited preemptive scheduling. There is no analysis for global scheduling, and there is no analysis for job-level fixed priority scheduling (which covers task-level fixed priority and EDF scheduling among others). We fill all these gaps in this paper.

Limited preemptive DAG tasks under both partitioned and global scheduling have been studied in the past for several scheduling policies [6]. The schedule abstraction graph (SAG) analysis [7] was shown to be the most accurate response time analysis for non-preemptive global scheduling of DAG tasks on multicore platforms [6], [7]. For that reason, in this work, we develop a response time analysis for global scheduling of limited-preemptive EDD tasks following the SAG principles.

Table I compares the capabilities of the analysis proposed in this paper to the state of the art. Besides the fact that the analysis proposed in this paper is the first for limited-preemptive EDD tasks, we highlight the following: Yalcinkaya's test does not return response time bounds (it is only a schedulability test), and both Yalcinkaya's and Casini's tests are limited to task-level fixed priority scheduling, when this paper can analyze the larger class of job-level fixed priority scheduling. Foughali's and Casini's tests are limited to single core or partitioned scheduling. Additionally, Foughali's test cannot analyze self-suspensions nor DAGs.

Contribution. In this work, we extend the schedule abstraction graph to develop the first response time analysis for limited-preemptive EDD tasks that are globally scheduled with a job-level fixed priority scheduling algorithm on a multicore platform. Doing so, we also have the following additional contributions: (1) we provide the first response time analysis for limited-preemptive self-suspending tasks under global joblevel fixed-priority scheduling, (2) we improve the accuracy of the response time analysis for limited-preemptive DAG tasks under global job-level fixed-priority scheduling in comparison to the state-of-the-art, and (3) we outperform the state-of-theart response time analysis for limited-preemptive scheduling of self-suspending tasks on single core.

The analysis proposed in this paper is flexible enough to support different task models, different scheduling policies (e.g., FP, EDF, ...) and analyze systems where execution segments (or jobs) of the same tasks may have the same or different priorities and deadlines, thus allowing to assign intermediate deadlines to subtasks and/or prioritizing more critical parts of an application over others.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this work, we consider a set T of n limited preemptive Event-Driven Delay-induced (EDD) tasks with known arrival patterns scheduled with a global work-conserving job-level fixed priority scheduling policy on m homogeneous cores.

Each task τ ∈ T is modeled as a DAG (V τ , E τ ), where V τ is the set of execution segments, and E τ ⊆ V τ ×V τ is the set of precedence constraints. Each vertex v ∈ V τ is labeled with the best-case execution time (BCET) C min τ,v and worstcase execution time (WCET) C max τ,v of the associated execution segment. Each directed edge e=(v, v ′ ) ∈ E τ connecting two vertices v and v ′ is labeled with a minimal delay sus min τ,v,v ′ and maximal delay sus max τ,v,v ′ (also referred to as minimal and maximal suspension time) between the execution of v and v ′ . The delays sus min τ,v,v ′ and sus max τ,v,v ′ model bounds on the duration of the waiting time between the completion of the execution of v and the notification of an event (or availability of a data) required to start the execution of v ′ .

Example 1. Consider an object detection task using radar and lidar data that offloads part of the computation on an FPGA to accelerate the treatment of the lidar points-cloud. Figure 1 shows how this task can be modeled as an EDD task. It starts with a node v 1 representing the execution of initialization code followed by two nodes v 2 and v 3 representing the treatment of the radar and lidar data in two parallel threads. The execution of v 2 and v 3 can directly start when v 1 completes, hence the minimum and maximum delay on the edges incoming those nodes are all 0. The data fusion requires both parallel sections v 2 and v 3 to be completed first. Since the lidar processing is partly offloaded to an FPGA, there is a delay between the completion of v 2 and the earliest time the data fusion may start. That delay is bounded by sus min τ,v2,v3 and sus max τ,v2,v3 as shown on the edge from v 2 to v 3 .

Note that, as already mentioned in [1], the EDD task model is a generalization of the self-suspending task model since a self-suspending task can simply be represented by an EDD task with a DAG made of a single path. Similarly, the EDD task model is also a generalization of DAG tasks since a DAG task is simply an EDD task where the minimum and maximum delay on each edge of the DAG always equal to 0.

We consider applications that need their tasks to be scheduled according to a deterministic arrival pattern (e.g., typical task chains in ROS2 [8] or Apollo Cyber RT [9] that are triggered by a timer, or more generally most tasks performing control, object recognition, obstacle detection, etc.). On each of its arrivals, the task releases one job for each execution segment in its set of vertices V .

Since the arrival pattern is assumed to be known beforehand, the problem reduces to the analysis of finitely many nonpreemptive jobs in a limited observation window. For example, if the tasks are periodic without offset and have constrained deadlines, then it is enough to analyze the jobs released in an observation window equal to a single hyperperiod. The observation window length can be adapted to the specific arrival pattern being analyzed. Therefore, our solution is not limited to the analysis of periodic tasks. Tasks with release bursts, multiframe tasks, multi-period tasks or any other tasks with predictable arrival patterns can also be analyzed.
We denote the set of jobs released in the observation window by J. Each job J ∈ J can be described by the tuple
div.formula: J = ([r min J , r max J ], [C min J , C max J ], d J , p J , pred J ),(1)
div.p: where r min J is the earliest release time, r max J is the latest release time, C min J is the best-case execution time (BCET), C max J is the worst-case execution time (WCET), d J is the absolute deadline, p J is the priority, and pred J ⊂ J is the set of immediate predecessors of J. Note that our model allows jobs released by different segments of the same task to have the same or different deadlines and/or priorities. This highlights the versatility of our model. We define succ J = {J ′ ∈ J | J ∈ pred J ′ } as the set of successors of J.

The priority p J of jobs is decided according to a joblevel fixed-priority (JLFP) scheduling policy. We say that J has higher priority than J ′ if p J < p J ′ , and assume that "<" implicitly reflects a tie-breaking rule (e.g., using the jobs identifiers). The exact value of the execution time
div.formula: C J ∈ [C min J , C max J
div.p: ] of a job is also unknown a priori, only bounds on the execution time, in the form of a best-case and worst-case execution time, are assumed to be known. The actual release time r J ∈ [r min J , r max J ] of each job J ∈ J is decided at runtime (for instance by the operating system based on the current computational load or because of the treatment of non-preemptive portions of the kernel code), whereas the release bounds r min J and r max J are computed offline based on the arrival pattern, the task offset and the release jitter of the task. We say that J is possibly released at time t if t ≥ r min J , and we say that J is certainly released at time t if t ≥ r max J . Given a job J, for each predecessor J ′ ∈ pred J , a minimal suspension time sus min (J ′ , J) and maximal suspension time sus max (J ′ , J) is defined. This suspension time is inherited from the minimal and maximal delay between two execution segments defined at the task level, i.e., the minimal and maximal delay labeled on each edge e ∈ E τ . Similar to the execution time, the actual suspension time value sus(J ′ , J) ∈ [sus min (J ′ , J), sus max (J ′ , J)] between the execution of two jobs with precedence constraints is unknown a priori.

We say that a job becomes ready if it is released, all predecessors finished their execution, and the suspension times have expired. The time point where a job becomes ready is denoted by ρ J = max{r J , max J ′ ∈pred J {f J ′ + sus(J ′ , J)}} where f J ′ is the time at which the predecessor J ′ finished.

In this paper, we consider a work-conserving nonpreemptive scheduler. That is, (i) whenever a processor is available and a job is ready, the highest priority ready job is dispatched on the available processor, and (ii) if a job is being executed it runs to completion (i.e., without preemption).

Since the scheduler is deterministic (i.e., it always takes the same scheduling decision for the same set of ready jobs and cores availability times), the sequence of scheduling decisions, and thus the finishing time f J of every job J ∈ J are uniquely defined for each execution scenario defined as follows.

Definition 1 (Execution scenario). An execution scenario is a concrete assignment of values for the release time, execution time and suspension times of every job in the jobset J, i.e., it is a set {γ J } ∀J∈J with
div.formula: γ J = (r J , C J , (sus(J ′ , J)) J ′ ∈pred J ),(2)
div.p: where
div.formula: r J ∈ [r min J , r max J ], C J ∈ [C min J , C max J ],
div.p: and sus(J ′ , J) ∈ [sus min (J ′ , J), sus max (J ′ , J)].
The set of all possible execution scenarios for job set J is denoted by Γ.

If the finishing time f J does not exceed the absolute deadline d J for all jobs J ∈ J in all execution scenarios γ ∈ Γ, then we say that the job set J (and by extension, the task set T) is schedulable. For ease of presentation, in this paper, we assume discrete time, i.e., all values are natural numbers, even though the analysis holds for continuous time.

div.head: III. ANALYSIS
div.p: We analyze the best-case and worst-case response time of each task in T by analyzing the best-case and worst-case response time of each job in J. To that end, similar to [7], [10], we explore the space of all possible schedules under all possible execution scenarios.

Note that the current version of the schedule abstraction graph is limited to tasks without suspension [7], [11]. Since self-suspending tasks, and thus the more general EDD task model, are inherently unintuitive, many problems appeared in the literature [12]. Therefore, careful treatment is required during the integration of such task model in the SAG analysis.

div.head: A. Schedule Abstraction Graph
div.p: The schedule abstraction graph (SAG) uses a graph to analyze all possible execution scenarios of a job set by abstracting all possible scheduling decisions taken by the scheduler and their influence on the system state. The information stored in the graph can then be used to analyze the best-case and worstcase response time of the jobs and their corresponding tasks. Each path in the SAG reflects a sequence of job scheduling decisions, and each node in the graph represents a possible state reachable by the system (see Fig. 2 for an example).

Each node N in the SAG abstracts the system state after the scheduling decisions described by the paths ending at that node. We define Γ(N ) ⊆ Γ as the subset of execution scenarios (i.e., the set of all concrete values combinations for the release, execution and suspension times of jobs in J) that are compatible with the job scheduling decisions described by the paths ending at N . An edge connecting a node N to Ñ in the graph represents a scheduling decision made by the scheduler to dispatch a job J that made the system state abstracted by N evolve to the new system state Ñ . The edge is then labeled with the job that was dispatched by the scheduler.

N abstracts a system state using the following information: 1) the set of jobs D that have already been dispatched for execution on a processor until reaching the system state abstracted by N , 2) m intervals [A min i , A max i ] for i = 1, . . . , m that model when the m cores will become available to execute new jobs when in the system state abstracted by N , 3) the finishing time interval [f min J , f max J ] for each job J ∈ D that was dispatched on a processor and has a successor that still needs to be executed, and 4) a set of at most m jobs χ ⊆ D that are certainly executing in the system state abstracted by N . The set of dispatched jobs D is simply an aggregation of all the jobs labeling the edges on any path that ends in N (since, according to the semantics of the SAG, the jobs that have been dispatched until reaching a system state are labeling the edges on the path to the node N ).

The cores availability intervals can be interpreted as follows. . Similarly, we can say that i cores possibly become available at time A min i , and i cores are certainly available at or after A max i . The set χ ⊆ D of certainly executing jobs contains at most m jobs (since there are only m cores in the platform) that are certainly running on the platform when the last job J ∈ D scheduled until reaching N started to execute. In other word, χ contains all jobs J ′ that finish later than the start time of J, i.e., χ = {J ′ ∈ D|f min J ′ > s J } where s j is the start time of job J and f min J ′ is the earliest finish time of job J ′ .

div.p: Example 2. Consider the set of jobs shown in Fig. 2 scheduled on a single core platform. Those jobs are released by two EDD tasks (or more specifically, by one sequential and one self-suspending task) with fixed priorities. The self-suspending task is made of three execution segments and has the highest priority. The sequential task has a single execution segment and the lowest priority. As shown in Fig. 2, job J 1 may have execution time variation (i.e., its BCET is 3 and WCET is 5), the two suspension intervals may vary in duration between 1 and 2 time units, and J 4 experiences release jitter and its release time may be any time in the interval [0,7]. Those execution, suspension and release time uncertainties mean that, even for such a small example of four jobs, there are many possible execution scenarios. To be precise, there are 96 different concrete assignments of values to the execution, suspension and release times of jobs. The SAG analyzing all those execution scenarios is shown in Fig. 2. As can be seen, the SAG can analyze the 96 possible execution scenarios and abstract all possible reachable system states with only 7 nodes. The SAG begins with an initial node N 0 , representing the state of the system prior to dispatching any job on the platform. Hence, the availability interval A 1 is [0, 0], meaning that the core is certainly available from time 0 onward. Since nothing has been scheduled yet, the set of dispatched jobs D and the set of certainly running jobs χ are both empty (Fig. 2 shows only χ as the content of D is given by all jobs appearing on the edges of paths ending at a node N ). Since, in our example, J 1 has the highest priority, and it is certainly released at time 0, the scheduler will always execute J 1 first in any execution scenario. Thus, J 1 is the sole eligible job for dispatch in the system state abstracted by N 0 . The SAG then contains a single new node N 1 succeeding N 0 . Since J 1 's execution time is within 3 to 5 time units, the availability interval of our single core becomes A 1 = [3,5] signifying that the core will possibly become available at time 3 and will certainly become available at time 5 after J 1 's execution. The set of dispatched jobs D 1 and certainly running jobs χ 1 in N 1 both contain J 1 . Note that all execution scenarios γ ∈ Γ will start with the system state N 0 followed by N 1 . Therefore, we say that both N 0 and N 1 account for all the execution scenarios and we write Γ(N 0 ) = Γ(N 1 ) = Γ. Once the system is in the state abstracted by N 1 , the scheduler may take two different scheduling decisions depending on when J 4 is released and when J 2 becomes ready to execute (i.e., when the suspension time following J 1 's completion ends). If J 4 is released before J 2 becomes ready, then J 4 is the next job dispatched, otherwise, J 2 is (since it has a higher priority). Therefore, there are two branches succeeding N 1 in the SAG, one with an edge labeled J 4 and one with an edge labeled J 2 . The availability interval of the core and the set of certainly running jobs in the resulting system states are then updated accordingly. Note that the set of execution scenarios Γ(N 2 ) accounted for by N 2 is now disjoint from the set of execution scenarios Γ(N 3 ) accounted for by N 3 . However, all possible scheduling decisions taken in the system state abstracted by N 1 are accounted for when expanding the graph after N 1 . Thus, we have Γ(N 2 ) ∪ Γ(N 3 ) = Γ(N 1 ) = Γ, meaning that all execution scenarios are accounted for at each "layer" of the SAG. The SAG is built using Alg. 1. It takes the jobset J as input and starts by initializing bounds on the best-case and worst-case response time of each job in J (Lines 2 to 4). It also creates the first initial node N 0 that represents the system state when no job has been dispatched on the platform yet (Line 5). Then, as already indicated in Example 2 above, the SAG is constructed in a depth-first manner, i.e., it is constructed layer by layer (Lines 6 to 32). The construction of each layer involves two phases: an expansion and a merging phase.

Expansion Phase: For each node on the last layer added to the SAG (called L cur in Alg. 1), all the potential next scheduling decisions are explored, i.e., for each node N i ∈ L cur , which jobs may be scheduled next in the system state abstracted by that node? (Lines 9 to 12). For every possible scheduling decision, i.e., for every job J that may be dispatched by the scheduler in a system state of the current layer L cur , a new system state is generated (Line 19) and added to the next layer of the SAG (called L next in Alg. 1). It is also at that step that the earliest and latest finish time of job J for all execution scenarios compliant with scheduling J in the system state N i are calculated. We use those values to update our bounds on the best-and worst-case response time of J and check that J meets its deadline. The details of the expansion phase are provided in Section III-B.

Merging Phase: To curb an explosion of the number of nodes in the SAG, we merge similar states in the same layer into a single node (Lines 20 to 25). The details of the merging phase are provided in Section III-C. The algorithm stops when there is no job left to schedule in the system states abstracted by the current layer. Note that Alg. 1 does not need to remember all nodes of the graph. It only requires remembering the nodes of the current and next layer that is being constructed.

Given a node N on the ℓ-th layer of the SAG, the generation of the nodes that result from dispatching all jobs that may be scheduled by the scheduler in the system state abstracted by N can be divided into 3 steps: 3) For every job J that may be started in the system state abstracted by N , generate a new node abstracting the new system state after scheduling J, and add it to the (ℓ + 1)-th layer of the SAG. 1) Potentially Ready Jobs: First, we have to decide which scheduling decisions are possible in the system state abstracted by a node N . That is, we have to determine which jobs may be started by the scheduler in the system state abstracted by N for any possible execution scenario in Γ(N ).

We know that only jobs J ∈ J \ D that have not been dispatched yet can be started next. Moreover, the job J that is started next must be ready when it is started. That is, all its predecessors pred (J) must have been dispatched, i.e., pred (J) ⊆ D. Therefore, we define the set R of potentially ready jobs as
div.formula: R := {J ∈ J \ D | pred (J) ⊆ D} .(3)

According to the system model, the release time r J and suspension time sus(J ′ , J) are within the interval [r min J , r max J ] and [sus min (J ′ , J), sus max (J ′ , J)], respectively. For f J ′ , as discussed in Sec. III-A, a lower and upper bound f min J ′ and f max J ′ are stored in the node N . Thus, a lower bound ρ min J and upper bound ρ max J on ρ J are given by:

div.p: A single job J is selected by the scheduler to be started next after the system state represented by N . There are two cases that must be considered:

Case 1: J is already ready when a processor becomes available. In that case, J has to be the ready job with the highest priority when the processor becomes available. Case 2: J is not ready when a processor becomes available.

In that case, no other jobs must have become ready before J becomes ready (otherwise, those other jobs would be executed first due to the work-conserving property of the scheduling policy). Moreover, when J becomes ready, no higher-priority jobs become ready at the same time. In the following, we consider those two cases to derive bounds for the starting time s J of the job J in the execution scenario γ.
Lemma 1. If J starts as described in Case 1, then the following bounds hold for the starting time s J of J:
div.formula: 1) ρ min J ≤ s J 2) A min 1 ≤ s J ≤ A max 1 3) s J < ρ max J ′ for all J ′ ∈ R with p J ′ < p J .
div.p: Proof. We prove the three properties in order.
1) By definition, a job cannot start to execute before it is ready. Therefore, ρ J ≤ s J , and thus ρ min J ≤ s J since ρ min J is a lower bound on ρ J .

2) According to the definition of Case 1, J is ready when the processor becomes available. Therefore, J is dispatched as soon as a processor becomes available. Since A min 1 and A max 1 are a lower and upper bound on when a processor becomes available, we must have
div.formula: s J ∈ [A min 1 , A max 1 ].
div.p: 3) There may be no higher priority job ready when J starts, otherwise the higher priority job would be dispatched instead of J. Hence,
div.formula: s J < ρ J ′ ≤ ρ max J ′ for all J ′ ∈ R with p J ′ < p J .

div.p: Proof. We prove the four properties in order.

1) According to the definition of Case 2, J is not ready when a processor becomes available. Therefore, J is started after the earliest time a processor may become available, that is, s J > A min 1 . 2) Since, according to the definition of Case 2, a processor is available when J becomes ready and no higher priority job is ready, J is started as soon as it becomes ready. Therefore, s J = ρ J implying ρ min J ≤ s J ≤ ρ max J . 3) Because a processor is available before J starts, if another job J ′ ∈ R was ready before J starts, then, by the work-conserving property, J ′ would be executed on the free processor instead of J. Therefore, s J ≤ ρ J ′ ≤ ρ max J ′ must hold for all J ′ ∈ R such that J ̸ = J ′ . 4) If another job J ′ ∈ R with higher priority than J was ready at or before J starts, then that other job would be executed instead of J. Therefore, s J < ρ J ′ ≤ ρ max J ′ must hold for all J ′ ∈ R with p J ′ < p J .

div.head: IV. CORRECTNESS
div.p: In this section, we prove that the SAG analyzes all possible execution scenarios for J and that it derives safe bounds on the response time of every job in each of those execution scenarios.
Theorem 1. The SAG analyzes all reachable system states in all possible execution scenarios in Γ.
Proof. We make a proof by induction that all system states reachable in an execution scenarios in Γ is in the SAG. That is, we prove N ∈Lℓ Γ(N ) = Γ for all ℓ = 0, 1, . . . .

Start case (ℓ = 0). In all execution scenarios the initial system state must be that all cores are free and no jobs has been dispatched yet. That states is abstracted by the initial node N 0 in the SAG. Furthermore, it yields N ∈L0 Γ(N ) = Γ where L 0 is the set of nodes in layer 0 of the SAG.

Induction step (ℓ → ℓ+1). If N ∈Lℓ Γ(N ) = Γ at the ℓ-th layer of the SAG, then we prove that layer ℓ + 1 contains all system states reachable from the system states recorded in the ℓ-th layer, and N ∈Lℓ+1 Γ(N ) = Γ. Since, for every node N in the ℓ-th layer, Alg. 1 adds a new system state in layer ℓ + 1 for every possible scheduling decision in all execution scenarios covered by N (Lines 10 to 27), we have that layer ℓ + 1 contains all system states reachable from N , and we have that Ñ ∈Lℓ+1 Γ( Ñ ) ⊇ Γ(N ) for all N ∈ L ℓ , which yields Ñ ∈Lℓ+1 Γ( Ñ ) ⊇ N ∈Lℓ Γ(N ) = Γ by the induction hypothesis. This proves our induction claim.

Conclusion. Since, by the induction step, every layer contains all system states reachable from the previous layer in all execution scenarios, all system states of all execution scenarios are eventually analyzed in the SAG. Proof. By Theorem 1, all reachable system states are part of the SAG. Since Alg. 1 computes a lower and upper bound on the finish time of each job scheduled in every system state in the SAG (Line 13), and because it returns the lowest and largest relative finish time it calculated in any system state for every job (Lines 14 and 15), the relative finish times returned for every job are real lower and upper bounds on the BCRT and WCRT of every job.

div.head: V. EVALUATION
div.p: Since our analysis is the first for limited-preemptive EDD tasks, there is no prior work we can compare our analysis against, as we are now setting the benchmark. Therefore, instead, we evaluate our analysis against the state of the art for self-suspending [3], [4] and DAG tasks [7]. In the following, we refer to [3] as Yalcinkaya, [4] as Casini, and [7] as Nasri.

We answer the following questions. How does our analysis compare against the state of the art response time analysis for limited-preemptive self-suspending tasks 1 and DAG tasks? What is the accuracy of our analysis in terms of schedulability? How well does it scale with the number of jobs and cores?

Experimental setup. We implemented our analysis in C++ using [13] as a basis but implementing a completely new analysis core that optimizes runtime. For each experiment, we generate n periodic tasks with implicit-deadline and without offset (n ∈ {4, 5, 8, 10, 12}) executed on m processors (m ∈ {1, 2, 4, 6}). To generate segmented self-suspending tasks, we randomly generate n "artificial" utilization values U ′ τ that sum to a target total utlization U ′ for the n tasks τ ∈ T using UUnifast [14]. We then randomly draw a period T τ for each task from a logarithmic distribution over the interval [10,10000]. We set the total WCET and the total worst-case suspension time of each task τ to C τ = β × U ′ τ × T τ and susp τ = (1-β)×U ′ τ ×T τ , respectively, where β is a parameter that defines the ratio of execution versus suspension. We then divide the total WCET between S execution segments, and the worst-case suspension time between S -1 suspension intervals using the randfixedsum algorithm [15], where S is a parameter of the experiment. The best-case execution time and best-case suspension time of each segment is set to 50% of their worstcase counterpart. Tasks are assigned priorities according to deadline monotonic. To increase the chance that the generated task sets are schedulable, we also limit the WCET of any execution segment to be at most half the smallest task period.
Each experiment is run on a single core of an Intel Xeon w7-3465x processor with peak frequency of 3.2GHz and equipped with 251GB of RAM.

Single-core scheduling. Since Casini can only analyze single core scheduling we start with an experiment for selfsuspending task scheduling on single core. Fig. 4a shows the number of task sets that were deemed schedulable by Yalcinkaya, Casini and our analysis out of 100 randomly generated task set per utilization value U ′ . Yalcinkaya is an exact schedulability analysis and it deems almost all task sets as being schedulable. Yalcinkaya, however, is not a response time analysis. Therefore, contrary to Casini and our analysis, it cannot provide response time bounds. However, Yalcinkaya's exactness allows us to check the real accuracy of Casini and our analysis in terms of schedulability.

Our analysis is able to detect around 90% of the schedulable task sets up to U ′ = 50% but the accuracy steadily decreases until around 50% at U ′ = 90%. It is still a significant gain in comparison to Casini, which can detect almost no schedulable task set at U ′ = 90%.

Runtime. Besides the fact that Yalcinkaya does not return response time bounds, the test [3] is known to suffer from scalability issues. Therefore, we test how our new analysis fares in terms of runtime against Yalcinkaya in a still rather simple setting by considering 5 tasks comprising 5 execution segments executed on two cores. Fig. 4f shows the average runtime and the number of experiments that timed out after 1 hour for each value of U ′ . None of the tests timed out with our analysis. In comparison, between 23 and 50% of the tests timed out with Yalcinkaya for almost every utilization value. The runtime of Yalcinkaya is also 4-6 orders of magnitudes larger than that of our analysis in average. It shows that our analysis scales much better and is thus more practical than the analysis proposed in [3] to analyze multicore systems. We also remind one more time that our analysis calculates more information than [3] as it also calculates best-case and worstcase response time bounds for every job where [3] only returns a boolean value for the schedulability.

To be noted that Foughali et al. [5] recently published an UPPAAL-based test that scales better than Yalcinkaya. Yet, the test in [5] can only analyze single core platforms and does not support self-suspensions. Still, to benchmark our analysis, we ran Foughali et al. [5] on the AUTOSAR use case2 available on their gitlab3 . Foughali's test requires 125 seconds to check the schedulability of seven limited-preemptive tasks made of 710 segments executed on a single core. According to our tests, it also requires between 125 and 165 seconds to calculate the worst-case response time bound for a task. In comparison, the test of Nasri available on GitHub [13] takes 244 seconds to calculate the exact worst-case but also the bestcase response times for every task as well as every job released in a hyper-period. Our new analysis solves the same problem and provides exact response time bound in only 4 seconds, thus showing almost two orders of magnitude improvement against Nasri and a 30X speedup in comparison to [17].

Thanks to those performances, our analysis could easily analyze systems of 8 cores running 10 tasks comprising 5 execution segments each with no time outs. The result of that experiment is shown in Fig. 4b. Again, we see that our analysis can identify a large number of schedulable task sets even at high utilization values.

In Fig. 4e, we provide the runtime of our analysis for various configurations of cores and tasks. This figure illustrates the impact of the number of jobs and cores on the runtime of the analysis. We observe that our approach can analyze the large majority of systems with up to 12 tasks on 6 cores under 2 minutes and some larger systems take up to an hour. This demonstrates the scalability of our analysis, especially as the number of cores and tasks increases.

In Fig. 4g, we illustrate the impact of the number of cores and number of tasks on the runtime of our analysis for varying utilisation values. The number of tasks was set to be twice the number of cores. We observe that the runtime of our analysis scales with the number of cores and tasks, but decreases as utilization values increase. This is because, with higher utilization, fewer schedulable task sets are found, meaning that the analysis does not need to explore the entire state space. Importantly, these results demonstrate that our analysis scales well with increasing number of cores and tasks, effectively handling the analysis of larger systems within the timeout limit.

Impact of β. We tested how the parameter β impacts schedulability. Fig. 4c shows that, non-surprisingly, schedulability decreases when the ratio β that controls the length of the execution segments versus the suspension ones increases. Since execution segments become longer, the blocking they may generate due to their non-preemptivity increases, making the schedulability drop.

Improvement of DAG analysis. We evaluated the improvement offered by our new version of the SAG analysis over the previous SAG analysis for DAG tasks, as presented in [7]. The DAG tasks were generated using the method described in [4], [18], with the probability of a node forking set to 0.6, a maximum of 2 nested forks, and up to 3 parallel segments originating from a fork. For this experiment, we generated 50 random task sets per utilization, for both Fixed Priority (FP) and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling policies, which was sufficient to demonstrate the improvement. The results, shown in Fig. 4d, indicate that the new system state abstraction used in our work significantly enhances analysis accuracy in comparison to Nasri, which was the best existing test for limited-preemptive DAG tasks until now. Our analysis was able to detect 2.5 times more schedulable tasksets for both FP and EDF scheduling poilicies than Nasri. Notably, this significant improvement did not come at the cost of increased runtime, on the contrary. Our analysis takes between 0.0001 and 2.22 seconds to analyze a task set with an average runtime of 0.36 seconds. In comparison, Nasri takes between 0.0013 and 139.68 seconds with an average of 4.42 seconds. Therefore, our analysis demonstrates a runtime improvement over Nasri of one order of magnitude in average and up to two orders of magnitudes in some cases. This is thanks to our new implementation of the SAG analysis core, which was rethought to optimize runtime.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORK
div.p: Self-suspending real-time tasks were first studied in [19], [20]. Since then, many results have been published [12], [21]. There are two main self-suspension models that have been predominantly studied: segmented [22]- [30] and dynamic selfsuspension [31]- [39]. Segmented self-suspending tasks are made of a sequence of execution and suspension segments with bounded duration. Dynamic self-suspension does not specify the number or duration of segments. Therefore, the segmented self-suspending task model allows for a more precise modeling of the specific execution behavior of a task when suspensions happen at well defined places in their code. Because key insights from classical timing analysis, like the critical instant theorem [40], do not hold for self-suspending tasks [12], many issues were found in the literature [12], [29], [30], [37], [41], thereby highlighting the need to carefully design any new response time analysis for self-suspending or EDD tasks.

Preemptive scheduling of self-suspending tasks has been extensively studied [31]- [33], [36], [39], [42]- [45]. As explained earlier, to the best of our knowledge, only two schedulability analyses [3], [4] for non-preemptive scheduling of selfsuspending tasks exist. [4] analyze fixed priority scheduling on single core and partitioned multicore. [3] focus their analysis on global multiprocessor scheduling using UPPAAL. Their schedulability analysis is exact but does not provide response time bounds. Our analysis is thus the first to provide response time bounds for limited-preemptive self-suspending tasks for job-level fixed priority scheduling on both single and multicore.

The real-time DAG task model was also extensively studied [6] since its introduction in [46]. Similarly to self-suspending tasks, preemptive scheduling received most of the attention with many analyses for different scheduling policies [47]- [53]. The conditional DAG task model was also presented in [18], [54] as an extension to the DAG model.

Results for limited-preemptive scheduling of DAG task is more sparse. The work in [7], [55] analyze global scheduling and [4] analyzes partitioned scheduling. The SAG-based analysis presented in [7] was shown to outperform the others for periodic tasks [6]. The SAG analysis is a framework that has been extended to analyze many different task models and type of systems [11], [56]- [58] always showing improved analysis performances at the cost of a larger runtime than more traditional response-time analyses.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we proposed the first response time analysis for limited-preemptive EDD tasks executed by a job-level fixed priority global scheduling algorithm on a single or multicore platform. The analysis extends the SAG approach to account for suspension times, proposing an updated SAG generation algorithm and a new system state abstraction.

The experimental results show that, on randomly generated task sets, our analysis outperforms the only other existing response time analysis for limited-preemptive self-suspending tasks. It outperforms the state of the art analysis for limitedpreemptive DAG tasks globally scheduled on a multicore platform. It also scales to the analysis of much larger systems than the exact schedulability test for self-suspending tasks by [3] or limited-preemptive tasks by [5] as shown on a realistic automotive case study derived from the WATERS17 industrial challenge [16].
